doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Aiming jazz musicians at commercial records
summary: Dorn says he tried to make jazz artists' records that could sell without losing their jazz chops. He names Cannonball and Creed Taylor as comparisons.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Well in a record like that, I don’t know what kind of — to put a label on it — but —
You tell me what you think it is.
Well it’s soul jazz to me.
Okay. Because my favorite group was Cannonball with —
Well Cannonball had the best balance ever between commercial and artistic. Ever.
Yeah. But what I’m wondering is with a record like that, how much thought is there to actually directing the music to sell LPs?
Don’t be polite. In other words, okay —
No, this we need a hit, you know.

Well because the guys that I recorded I thought were capable of having hits. Listen. I’m not going to out-Blue Note Blue Note. I’m not going to out-Verve Verve, and I’m not going to out-Prestige Prestige. They did something. I wanted to make records with guys who you call jazz musicians who I think could sell records and not lose their jazz chops. So I wasn’t the first or the only guy but I was — maybe me and Creed Taylor were the only two people who were like really chasing commercial records. Because he had done like incredible work at Verve and stuff in a non-commercial area but with great successes that became commercial like Getz’s stuff you know, and things like that. But I wanted to make records that people could like enjoy as records. If you want the real jazz chops, I did some real jazz records, but Fathead took all those solos with Ray Charles. You know he was capable of having a hit record.
